'''''Honckenya peploides''''', the '''sea sandwort''' (UK) or '''seaside sandplant''' (Canada),<ref>[http://www.cbif.gc.ca/pls/itisca/next?v_tsn=19970&taxa=&p_king=every&p_string=containing&p_ifx=cbif&p_lang= Integrated taxonomic information system (ITIS).  (2009). Retrieved August/04, 2010]</ref> is the only [[species]] in the [[genus]] '''''Honckenya''''' of the plant family [[Caryophyllaceae]]. Other common names include '''sea chickweed''', '''sea pimpernal''', '''sea-beach sandwort''',<ref>{{cite book|author=Nowick, Elaine|title=Historical Common Names of Great Plains Plants Volume I: Historical Names (paperback)|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HTTaCQAAQBAJ&pg=PA354 |year=2014 |publisher=Lulu.com |isbn=978-1-60962-058-5 |page=354}}</ref> and '''sea purslane'''.<ref>{{citation |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=115719 |title=Flora of North America |author=Warren L. Wagner |chapter=''Honckenya'' Ehrhart, Neues Mag. Aerzte. 5: 206. 1783.}}</ref> The scientific name is often spelled "''Honkenya''", and is named after the German botanist [[Gerhard August Honckeny]] (or Honkeny).<ref>{{cite book |author=Le Roy Abrams |author2=Roxana Stinchfield Ferris |name-list-style=amp |year=1923 |series=An Illustrated Flora of the Pacific States |volume=2 |title=Polygonaceae to Krameriaceae, buckwheats to kramerias |publisher=[[Stanford University Press]] |isbn=9780804700047}}</ref> This plant has a [[Circumboreal Region|circumboreal]] [[Range (biology)|distribution]].

The plant is a [[succulent]] perennial growing at the edge of the sea. It has small greenish white [[pentamerous]] flowers with 10 [[stamen]]s in the male flowers borne in the leaf axils.<ref>''New Flora of the British Isles'', [[Clive Stace]], 2005, Cambridge University Press</ref> The fruit capsule opens in three valves.

==Description==
''Honckenya peploides'' is a small, subdioecious, spreading plant, forming patches on sand and shingle above the high water mark of beaches. The stem is branching and buried in the sand. The leaves grow in opposite pairs and are fleshy with membranous margins, pale yellowish-green and ovate, oblong or lanceolate, usually with pointed tips. The flowers are often [[Dioecy|dioecious]] and have parts in fives. They grow in the upper leaf axils and have ovate to lanceolate sepals, greenish-white petals of about the same length, and three styles. The fruit is a capsule larger than the sepals and superficially resembling a pea. In pistillate flowers the stamens are undeveloped while in staminate flowers, the capsules are poorly developed.<ref name=Hulten/><ref>{{cite book |title=The Concise British Flora in Colour |last=Keble Martin |first=W |year=1965 |publisher=Ebury Press |page=16 }}</ref>

There are two subspecies, ''H. p. peploides'' is the nominate subspecies with ovate to lanceolate leaves and flowers growing singly in the upper leaf axils, while ''H. p. major'' is coarser, has longer, more slender leaves, and the flowers are mostly in a multi-flowered cyme.<ref name=Hulten>{{cite book|author=Hultén, Eric|title=Flora of Alaska and Neighboring Territories: A Manual of the Vascular Plants|url=https://archive.org/details/floraofalaskanei0000hult |url-access=registration|year=1968 |publisher=Stanford University Press |isbn=978-0-8047-0643-8 |page=[https://archive.org/details/floraofalaskanei0000hult/page/434 434]}}</ref>

==Distribution==
[[File:Honkenya peploides, Anglesey.jpg|thumb|left|Sea sandwort on a beach in Anglesey]]
''Honckenya peploides'' has a circum-boreal distribution in both temperate and arctic regions. It is found in coastal regions on sand, shingle and pebbles, in northern Europe (including Britain), northern Asia and North America.<ref name=PFAF/>

==Research==
Clumps of ''Honckenya peploides'' of one sex (with either staminate or pistillate flowers) may be separated by a few metres or hundreds of metres from clumps of the other sex. Researchers in Spain studied whether these clumps exhibited different ecophysiological traits which made them better adapted to different microhabitats. They found that shoots growing near the edge of the clumps had higher photosynthetic efficiency and chlorophyll content. Growth rates between clumps of the different sexes did not differ significantly from each other, and male plants continued to have reproductive costs associated with flowering after the female plants had ceased to flower and the seeds were ripening.<ref>{{cite book|title=Sexual dimorphism in ecological and physiological traits in the subdioecious dune plant Honckenya peploides (L.) Ehrh.| date=2007 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mg2eA-gFlMEC&pg=PA63|publisher=Univ Santiago de Compostela |pages=63–|id=GGKEY:QTWHGSU6WGF}}</ref>

==Uses==
Both the leaves and the seeds of ''H. peploides'' are used as food.<ref name=PFAF/> The shoots and leaves are rich in [[vitamin A]] and [[vitamin C]] and can be used as a [[Leaf vegetable|green leafy vegetable]] either raw or cooked. They can also be fermented to prepare a [[sauerkraut]]-like preserve, and in Iceland are fermented in whey to produce a drink. The seeds are small in size and time-consuming to gather; they can be ground up and added to flour or used as a garnish.<ref name=PFAF>{{cite web |url=https://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Honckenya+peploides |title=Honckenya peploides – (L.)Ehrh. |publisher=Plants for a Future |access-date=24 June 2016}}</ref>
